analysis.one_liner: Makes the president repay taxpayers for business-travel security costs and bars presidential business activity in office.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat with three House committees since its introduction in December 2025, with no hearings or votes and only 4 cosponsors of 217 House Democrats.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require the president to pay the Treasury back for Secret Service protection and other government costs whenever travel serves the business interests of a company the president owns, controls, or profits from. It would also bar the president from creating, running, or sitting on the board of any business while in office, tax any income from such activity at 100%, ban soliciting donations for a presidential library while in office, and require the president's immediate family to report quarterly if they run businesses in ways the president is barred from. The bill also removes the president's and vice president's protection from certain lawsuits under the Federal Tort Claims Act. It was introduced in December 2025 and referred to three House committees.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers benefit if the bill passes: money spent protecting the president on trips that serve his own businesses would flow back to the Treasury instead of being absorbed by the public. Ordinary citizens also gain a check on a sitting president personally profiting from office, and the library-donation ban and family reporting rules would make money moving around a president more visible.

how_it_helps.text: It requires the president and vice president to reimburse the Treasury for Secret Service protection and other government costs incurred when they travel to promote or benefit businesses they own, control, or profit from.
It bars the president from creating, operating, or serving on the board of any business while in office, and taxes any income from such activity at 100% if it happens anyway.
It blocks the president from soliciting donations for a presidential library or museum while in office, and requires annual disclosure of those dealings to the Archivist of the United States.

It requires immediate family members who engage in business conduct the president is barred from to file quarterly reports to Congress and certify that their conduct is not enriching the sitting president.
It strips the president and vice president of Federal Tort Claims Act exceptions, allowing them to be sued for claims they could otherwise block.

analysis.who_pays: The president's own business interests pay if the bill passes — through repayment of security and travel costs, the 100% tax on any business income earned in office, and the ban on creating or operating a business while president. Family members who run businesses would bear new quarterly reporting and certification duties, and presidential library fundraisers would lose the sitting president as a solicitor of donations.

drawbacks.text: The 100% tax on any business income the president earns and the blanket ban on creating or operating a business while in office are broad rules that would apply to any future president, not just the current situation, and critics would say they go further than traditional conflict-of-interest practice, where officials typically divest or use blind trusts rather than be barred from all business activity.

Reimbursing the Secret Service for protecting the president on business-related travel puts the protective agency in the position of sorting which trips are official and which serve private interests, and a refusal to pay could complicate security decisions; the bill also caps the reporting penalty at $1,000 per day, which may be too small to compel compliance from a wealthy entity.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are real but hard to measure: reimbursement recovers public money and the business restrictions close an open channel between the presidency and private profit. The costs are modest — the Secret Service and Justice Department would need new billing and enforcement machinery, and the daily fine is a light penalty ($1,000 a day against a wealthy entity). The honest objection is scope: the bill targets the president's conduct broadly, and defenders of any administration would argue it risks entangling the Secret Service in politics and could be applied to a future president's pre-existing assets. It does nothing about conflicts already structured outside day-to-day operations, such as a president holding assets through a trust.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to three House committees and has sat there since, with no hearings or votes; Congress is still in session so it is technically alive.

narrative.text: The Stop Padding Presidential Pockets Act was introduced on December 17, 2025 by Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman (D-NJ), along with Reps. McIver and Tlaib.

The only action taken was referral on the day of introduction to the Oversight and Government Reform, Judiciary, and Ways and Means Committees, with consideration deferred to a later date determined by the Speaker.
Four Democrats cosponsored the bill, out of 217 House Democrats.
No hearings, markups, or votes are recorded; Congress remains in session through January 3, 2027, so the bill is still technically pending.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has gained or lost anything — the bill has produced no hearings, votes, or changes to presidential disclosure or travel reimbursement rules.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; the bill has not moved

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: No action recorded: the bill has sat in its three assigned committees since referral with no hearings, markups, or floor scheduling.

sides.party_line_note: All sponsors and cosponsors are Democrats (4 of 217 House Democrats); no Republicans have signed on and no votes have occurred, so the partisan shape so far is entirely one-sided sponsorship.

industries.industry: The president's family business empire (Trump Organization and similar private entities)
industries.note: The bill would force repayment of Secret Service costs on business-related travel, ban the president from operating or joining any business while in office, and tax any such income at 100%. Family members would face quarterly disclosure and certification requirements. It strikes directly at the practice of a sitting president profiting from a private business empire while in office.

The bill would bar the sitting president from soliciting donations for a presidential library and require the private entities that run them to report their financial dealings to the Archivist of the United States, with $1,000-a-day fines for missing reports. This adds disclosure and limits the flow of large donations to a sitting president's future library.

analysis.trajectory: First-term bills referred to three committees with a handful of cosponsors and no hearings rarely move; unless the Oversight Committee holds a hearing or the bill attracts dozens more cosponsors, it is likely to sit until the Congress ends in January 2027.
